title: What Affects Garden Room Costs? | Tom Cutts, Lancashire
description: Understand what changes a garden room quotation: size, foundations, access, insulation, glazing and services. Plan your project with Tom Cutts in Colne.
heading: What affects the cost of a garden room?
summary: A useful garden-room budget starts with how you want to use the space and what needs doing on your site. Here are the decisions to work through before comparing quotations.
photoAlt: Brown-clad garden room with dark-framed door and glazing from the Tom Cutts project gallery
body:
Start with the room you need

A quiet office, a hobby studio and a space for occasional summer use can have different requirements. Write down who will use the room, what needs to fit inside it and whether you expect to use it throughout the year. A sketch showing a desk, exercise equipment or seating often says more than an external measurement on its own.

There is no single price that accurately describes every bespoke garden room. Tom prepares a quotation around the agreed project. The points below help you understand what to include in that conversation.

Six things to discuss when setting a budget

  1. Size and layout. Discuss the usable space inside, door positions, storage and room for furniture. A larger footprint also changes the amount of foundation, structure, roof and finishing work.
  2. The site and its preparation. Share photographs of the proposed position, changes in level, existing structures and the surrounding ground. The support and foundation approach needs to suit the site and design.
  3. Access. Narrow gates, steps or a route through the house are useful details to flag early. Explain where deliveries can arrive and how materials can reach the garden.
  4. Comfort and finish. Discuss insulation, ventilation, glazing, cladding, internal linings and flooring together. Ask what is included in the quoted specification and what is an option.
  5. Power and other services. List the lighting, sockets, internet connection or other services you need. Confirm who supplies, installs and checks specialist work, and whether it sits within the main quotation.
  6. The outdoor space. Decking, steps, paths, a pergola or changes to the surrounding garden should be identified separately so that you can see the whole project cost.

Compare the same scope

Two quotations with the same room dimensions may cover different work. Ask for a written description of the materials, preparation, installation and finish. Check whether waste removal, delivery, services, decoration and any applicable VAT are included, excluded or still to be confirmed.

A lower headline figure is difficult to judge until these details line up. It is also useful to separate essential work from optional finishes, so that any changes to the budget are deliberate.

What to send with your enquiry

  • Your postcode and photographs of the proposed position and access.
  • Approximate dimensions, plus a simple sketch if you have one.
  • How you want to use the room and the furniture or equipment it needs to hold.
  • Your preferred finish, rough budget and any timing constraints.
  • Any drawings, site information or permissions advice you already have.

Ask at the outset which permissions, specialist design or other checks your project needs and who will arrange them. Those questions should be resolved for your particular site before work is agreed.

Plan the room and deck together

If you are considering both, discuss the entrance, seating area and route back to the house as one layout. The room and deck can then be quoted clearly, with the boundaries of each part of the work explained. Browse our garden-room and decking photographs, choose the details you like and send them with your enquiry.

title: Timber or Composite Decking? | Tom Cutts, Lancashire
description: Compare timber and composite decking by appearance, care, product quality and the complete installation. Practical questions for your Lancashire garden.
heading: Timber or composite decking?
summary: The right choice depends on the look you want, the particular product, your garden and the care you are happy to give it. Compare a complete deck specification, rather than a board price alone.
photoAlt: Garden decking with broad steps down to paving from the Tom Cutts project gallery
body:
Choose the appearance you want to live with

Timber offers natural grain and variation. The species, treatment and finish affect its appearance and suitability outdoors. The Timber Decking & Cladding Association explains that the words hardwood and softwood describe groups of trees; they are not a simple ranking of how durable a board will be. Read the TDCA timber guidance.

Composite boards offer manufactured finishes in a range of colours and profiles. Products differ, so look at samples of the actual range being quoted. Consider them beside your brickwork, garden room and paving, rather than choosing from a small picture alone.

Understand the care involved

Both types need cleaning. Leaves, dirt and surface growth can affect a deck, particularly in shaded or damp areas. The TDCA recommends regular cleaning for timber and wood-plastic composite surfaces; it also notes that decorative timber coatings need refreshing to maintain their appearance. Follow the care instructions for the specific board and finish. See the TDCA maintenance advice.

Some composite ranges avoid routine painting or staining. That does not mean every product is maintenance-free. Ask which cleaning products are suitable, what could damage the surface and what to do if an individual board needs attention.

Check claims against the actual product

Do not assume all composite boards perform alike. Formulations and designs vary, and the supporting structure and installation must suit the chosen system. Ask to see its installation instructions, care guidance and written warranty. The TDCA explains why product-specific evidence matters.

Think about the conditions in your garden. Manufacturer Trex, for example, says its decking can become slick in wet or icy weather and that its boards can get hot in direct sun. Those are reasons to discuss exposure and use, rather than accept a blanket claim of a surface being slip-proof or always cool. See Trex’s product FAQs. This is an example of manufacturer guidance, not a claim that a particular brand is included in your quotation.

Compare the cost of the finished deck

The board is only one part of the job. Ask each quotation to identify the area, preparation, supporting frame, boards, fixings, edges, steps and any guarding or additional work. The layout and access can affect the installation as well as the material choice.

A sensible comparison uses the same dimensions and scope. If one option costs more, ask exactly what changes in the product, finish or construction. Avoid choosing on a headline price that leaves essential parts of the job unlisted.

Five questions to bring to Tom

  • Which material and finish suit the look of my house and garden?
  • What care does this exact board need?
  • How does the design deal with the site, levels and access?
  • What is included in the complete installation price?
  • What written product and workmanship information will I receive?

Send your postcode, approximate dimensions and photographs of the space. Include how you want to use the deck: dining, seating, access to a garden room or another purpose. Tom can then discuss options around the actual project.

title: Garden Room & Decking Quote Checklist | Tom Cutts
description: A practical checklist for comparing garden room and decking quotations: scope, materials, access, specialist work, payment stages and handover details.
heading: What should your garden-project quotation include?
summary: A clear quotation helps you understand the work, compare options and agree what happens next. Use these questions when planning a garden room, decking or a combined outdoor project.
photoAlt: Timber framing during construction from the Tom Cutts project gallery
body:
1. A description of the agreed work

Start with the purpose of the project, its position and approximate dimensions. Ask for the main materials and finishes to be named. For a garden room, that might include cladding, glazing, internal finish and the services being considered. For decking, it includes the board specification, layout, edges and steps.

Photographs and a simple marked-up sketch can help explain the discussion. If drawings or specialist design are needed, establish who provides them and how they become part of the agreed scope.

2. Site preparation and access

Discuss what is already in the space and what must happen before construction. Existing structures, changes in ground level and the access route all need to be understood. Confirm what the quotation includes for preparation, deliveries, storage of materials, protection of surrounding areas and disposal of waste.

3. Inclusions, exclusions and choices

Make it easy to see which items are included, which are optional and which sit outside the quotation. A room price may need to be considered alongside specialist services, decoration, flooring or work to the surrounding garden. Ask whether applicable VAT is included and whether any amount is an allowance that still needs a final selection.

If you are combining a room and a deck, ask for the relationship between them to be clear. This helps you compare a complete project with quotations that cover only one part.

4. Responsibilities and checks

Agree who will coordinate the job and who handles any specialist work, permissions enquiries or design checks that the project requires. Ask what information you need to supply and which decisions must be made before a start can be arranged. The answer should relate to your site and planned use.

5. Timing and changes

Discuss the proposed programme, the factors it depends on and how progress will be communicated. If you change a material, add work or choose a different layout, ask how the revised scope, cost and timing will be recorded before that work goes ahead.

A clear written change avoids two different understandings of what was agreed. Keep the original quotation, selections and later amendments together.

6. Payment and handover

Ask for the payment stages and their associated milestones to be explained before agreeing to proceed. At handover, confirm what care information, product paperwork, specialist documentation or workmanship terms apply to your particular project. Keep a note of how to raise any outstanding questions.

A simple brief to copy into your enquiry

My postcode:
I’m planning: a garden room / decking / both
Approximate dimensions:
I’ll use the space for:
Access or site details:
Preferred materials or examples:
Rough budget:
Preferred timing:

Add a few photographs of the space and the route to it. You can send these to Tom on WhatsApp, or use the website form to start the conversation. We work from Colne across Pendle, the Ribble Valley and the surrounding service areas shown on the website.
